narrative.text: The cover page of the Spanish edition of WHO's guidance for countries on preparing to introduce human papillomavirus vaccines.
The title page of the Spanish edition of WHO's policy and programme guidance on preparing to introduce HPV vaccines.

The copyright page of the Spanish edition, © World Health Organization 2006, with standard WHO disclaimers; it still contains draft placeholders such as a bracketed note to name the expert group and 'Printed in …'.

The table of contents of the Spanish edition, listing sections from cervical cancer and HPV infection through vaccines, target groups, communication, service delivery, monitoring, stewardship and financing; most page numbers are placeholders ('xx').

Acknowledgements for the Spanish edition, explaining that the document draws on a technical consultation on sexual and reproductive health and HPV vaccination programmes held in Montreux, Switzerland, on 14–16 March 2006, and listing the participating experts and WHO departments.

Introduces the guidance, in Spanish, explaining that it comes from a UNFPA–WHO consultation and is meant to inform those working in sexual and reproductive health, immunization, adolescent health and cancer control about HPV vaccine introduction. It describes the burden of cervical cancer and notes that wide screening coverage has greatly reduced deaths in high-income countries.

Summarizes, in Spanish, World Health Assembly resolution WHA58.22 on cancer prevention and control, which stresses the importance of cervical cancer control, and includes a figure on HPV infection and cervical cancer by women's age.

Describes, in Spanish, the two prophylactic HPV vaccines, which trials showed to be highly effective in women aged 16–24 not previously exposed to the virus, and notes that HPV types 16 and 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers. It reports the licensing status of Gardasil and the expected approval of Cervarix in 2006.

Notes, in Spanish, that follow-up of phase III trial participants continues to answer open questions relevant to vaccination programmes, such as duration of protection, and includes a figure on HPV types in women with cancer by region.

Explains, in Spanish, that HPV vaccines are expected to be licensed first for girls and women aged 9–26, with stronger immune responses in younger girls. It notes that effects in women over 25 or already infected with types 16 or 18 still need study and that cost-effectiveness for these groups is unknown.

Links HPV vaccination, in Spanish, to WHO's 2004 Global Reproductive Health Strategy and its core aspects of sexual and reproductive health. It notes that, unlike vaccines such as rubella or tetanus, HPV vaccines will draw immunization programmes into sensitive issues of adolescent sexuality.

A footnote page, in Spanish, explaining that hepatitis B vaccine was added to immunization programmes without links to cancer control because infection mainly occurs in early childhood, and noting the difficulty of extending immunization beyond infants to older groups.

Summarizes, in Spanish, the UNICEF–WHO Global Immunization Vision and Strategy, which aims by 2015 for immunization to be a high priority and equitably available to all ages. It notes that efforts to prevent and control cervical cancer have so far been limited.

Argues, in Spanish, that experience introducing HPV vaccines could serve as a model for a future HIV vaccine and is relevant to the HIV community. It discusses the unique opportunity and high cost of HPV vaccines, warning that private-sector introduction could favour better-off groups and high- and middle-income countries.

Warns, in Spanish, that uneven introduction could widen health inequities, calling for strong public–private partnerships. It discusses how vaccination strategy must reflect each country's circumstances and the possible delays between licensing, affordable pricing and adequate supply in developing countries.

Discusses, in Spanish, the challenges of designing balanced advocacy, information and communication on HPV vaccination for varied audiences. It lists key facts to convey, such as that most HPV infections cause no symptoms and can be passed on unknowingly.

Continues the key messages, in Spanish, noting that the vaccines are highly effective in unexposed women aged 16–26 and expected to prevent up to 70% of cervical cancers, best given before first sexual contact. It stresses that national data on cervical cancer burden, HPV types and age at first sex should guide policy.

Sets out, in Spanish, the elements of a communication strategy on cervical cancer control and HPV vaccines aimed at decision makers, health professionals, women and communities, timed to national decisions. It lists what information to give target groups, such as indications, safety and side-effects.

Continues the communication guidance, in Spanish, stressing that vaccination does not imply stigma or that a girl is sexually active and setting out what is still unknown, such as use in women with HIV or pregnant women. It suggests linking messages to existing adolescent programmes such as school-based sexual health, nutrition, tobacco and HIV prevention education.

Discusses, in Spanish, reaching target groups, with a likely licensed age range of 9–26 divided into a priority group of girls aged 9–13 and a catch-up group. It weighs delivery through schools, health services and community programmes, including challenges in extending the cold chain to adolescent programmes.

Continues the discussion of service delivery, in Spanish, noting that staff of youth programmes may lack vaccination skills but that programmes for out-of-school youth can raise awareness and refer young people to vaccination services. It suggests using contacts such as prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission services to inform women about cervical cancer, HPV vaccines and screening.

Stresses, in Spanish, that older women outside the vaccine's age limits still need comprehensive cervical cancer screening, diagnosis and treatment, and that vaccinated girls must also be screened later. It begins discussing the need to plan monitoring and evaluation from the preparatory stage.

Explains, in Spanish, that effects of the quadrivalent vaccine on genital warts and early lesions will be seen before effects on cervical cancer and that pilot studies may help early evaluation. It lists actions on service delivery, starting with basing strategies on what is feasible and culturally acceptable in each country.

Continues the list of actions, in Spanish, such as extending immunization services to older age groups, aligning messages with cervical cancer, adolescent health and HIV programmes, monitoring vaccine effectiveness, training health workers and defining process and outcome indicators.

Discusses, in Spanish, stewardship and financing, giving high priority to mobilizing international and national resources to strengthen health systems and buy HPV vaccines as part of a comprehensive multi-partner strategy. It notes that national decisions should consider benefits not captured in health and cost analyses.

Stresses, in Spanish, the importance of international funding commitments for HPV vaccines through GAVI, UNICEF and the PAHO Revolving Fund, to encourage manufacturers to expand production capacity and to lower prices. It also covers regulatory tasks after licensing, such as adverse event reporting by the private sector and pharmacovigilance.

Lists, in Spanish, actions on stewardship and financing, such as forming a national working group with broad stakeholder participation to prepare an HPV vaccine introduction strategy and planning for financial sustainability. Countries not eligible for GAVI funding are advised to seek WHO and UNFPA technical help.

Concludes, in Spanish, that the decision on whether and when to introduce HPV vaccination rests with national policies and that effective alliances are needed because the vaccines span several programmes. It ends with a note on the conditions for which the quadrivalent vaccine was licensed by the US FDA.
Lists, in Spanish, additional resources, with website links for UNFPA, WHO, the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy and GAVI.
A page with no extracted text.
